title: Why Did XOM, CVX, MPC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of energy companies Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM), Chevron Corp. (CVX), and Marathon Petroleum Corp. (MPC) surged to annual highs on Monday as oil prices rallied amid growing geopolitical tensions. Brent crude prices touched nearly $110 a barrel on Monday as tensions in the Middle East continued to ratchet up. A series of recent escalations, including attacks on commercial ships near the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine’s strike on a Russian refinery, stoked fears about a further constraint in fuel supplies, sending prices higher. Worries continued despite the U.S. government’s efforts to curtail rising prices, including planned fuel releases and changes to U.S. sanctions on Russian imported fuel. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, energy prices have been climbing steadily, boosting energy companies. As per Koyfin data, energy stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by a significant margin in 2026. Exxon Mobil, Chevron, and Marathon Petroleum shares surged to 52-week highs on Monday before closing lower amid the steep climb in oil prices. XOM stock hit an annual high of $179.30 during trading hours on Monday before closing about 0.4% down. CVX stock surged to a 52-week high of $225.67, but ended the session 0.28% lower. MPC stock rallied to a 52-week high of $493.98 during regular trading, but finished the day nearly 1% down. Retail sentiment around XOM, CVX and MPC stocks was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing on Stocktwits. XOM stock has gained more than 48% year-to-date, while CVX and MPC stocks have surged more than 47% and 200%, respectively. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Retail investors in Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) are floating multibillion-dollar buyout scenarios and steep share-price gains after CEO Angelos Stergiou marked the company’s 15th anniversary with a post about its “next chapter.” SLS stock jumped 5% on Monday to $10.49, snapping three straight losing sessions. In his LinkedIn post, Stergiou reflected on Sellas’ growth from a private startup into a public biotech advancing investigational cancer treatments GPS and SLS009. “Reaching 15 years isn't just about celebrating our history; it is about stepping into our next chapter with even greater focus, drive, and resolve,” he said. He acknowledged past setbacks and thanked shareholders, employees and trial participants, while reaffirming the company’s commitment to patients. “Our mission remains deeply personal, and our promise to the patients we aim to serve is steadfast. We look forward, God willing, to the best chapters that are still to be written with GPS and SLS009,” he added. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SLS slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid a 258% jump in 24-hour message volumes. One user said: “My opinion, Dr. Stergiou’s message was a master-class at reassuring EVERYONE that all is well.” A user also floated a minimum $40 billion valuation. Another user argued for a $50 billion valuation, calling a $247-per-share figure. A separate user proposed a $120 billion buyout scenario and also predicted a share price of $540-plus. Across bullish share-price predictions, including scenarios tied to clinical results, targets ranged from $100 to over $540. Discussing buyout news in case of favorable data, one user said: “If BO news post good data then there’s no stopping this beast (really no explanation required as it could go full berserker mode).” BO means buyout. Another user challenged the lofty valuations and said: “I will be so glad to get out of this ticker when it hits $15 again.” The CEO’s message comes as investors have been searching for potential deal signals in recent months. In June, a filing disclosed changes to executive severance arrangements, including lump-sum payment provisions for Stergiou. For CFO John Burns and chief development officer Dragan Cicic, qualifying departures within one month before or one year after a change of control would trigger 15 months of salary, the annual target bonus, up to 18 months of health-coverage reimbursements and full vesting of unvested equity. Sellas’ conference plans have provided another talking point. The company is listed at Booth 138, with a 20-by-30-foot space, for the Dec.12- Dec.15 American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. Major exhibitors include Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Merck, AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb. The booth size has fueled speculation about a partnership or acquisition. Currently, investors are awaiting data from Sellas’ two lead programs. The Phase 3 Regal trial is testing GPS, an immunotherapy targeting WT1, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients who achieved a second complete remission following salvage treatment. Its final-analysis process is triggered by 80 deaths. Sellas reported 78 events as of May 11. Reaching 80 precedes database lock, data review and analysis before results are disclosed. The company also expects fourth-quarter topline data from its 80-patient Phase 2 SLS009 study in newly diagnosed AML, including patients with early resistance to azacitidine and venetoclax. SLS009 is also being explored in pancreatic cancer. Preclinical findings from last month showed 17.9% apoptosis (programmed cell death) in a patient-derived tumor model resistant to Daraxonrasib, versus 2.8% with Daraxonrasib alone. Combining the drugs raised apoptosis to 36.5% and necrosis to 30.6%. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. U.S. stock futures climbed into positive territory late Monday as technology stocks rebounded after a sharp selloff last week. Meanwhile, markets are keenly watching the third-quarter (Q3) earnings season unfold, with about 70 S&P 500 companies slated to report earnings this week. As of 11:13 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.25%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.21% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.15%. On Monday, the three benchmark indexes closed mixed. The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding more than 290 points to close 1.11% higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.41% at close, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.07%. Technology and AI stocks were top of mind for markets on Monday as the sector reversed last week's steep selloff. Chip stocks led the climb on Monday. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) closed up nearly 2%, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) closed up 1.61%. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Micron Technology Inc. (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) all ended the session in green. The run comes ahead of vital Q3 results that will follow this week, which are likely to set the tone for the trajectory of technology shares. “Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration,” Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, said in a note, according to CNBC. Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, reportedly said in a note on Monday that the week will be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support, while noting that a hold is possible amid widespread, short-term oversold conditions. Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) are due to report Q3 results later this week, while multiple other semiconductor and technology companies, including Lam Research (LRCX) and Texas Instruments (TXN), will also post their results. AI-related power companies Bloom Energy (BE) and Valero Energy (VLO), along with big entertainment companies including Netflix Inc. (NFLX), will also announce their quarterly results. Meanwhile, rising oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainty have put downward pressure on markets. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $109.88 a barrel, up about 0.3%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $103.64 per barrel. Economist Peter Schiff said in a post on X, “Oil rose another 2.5% today. It's almost $104. If you think gas prices are high now, just wait until after the midterms when Trump has to turn off the spigots from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to keep it from running dry. Oil could hit $150, sending gas prices to record highs.” Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (DJT): Shares of the president’s media company were in focus late Monday after the stock slipped 8%, its worst single-day drop since February, as President Donald Trump’s approval rating hit a record low. Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN): The company’s stock surged nearly 5% at close on Monday and continued to climb higher overnight after Morgan Stanley raised its price target and named it a ‘Top Pick.’ Cerebras Systems Inc. (CBRS): The AI hardware and supercomputing company was on the retail radar after shares slipped more than 5% on Monday, extending a broader selloff in the sector from last week. CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV): Shares of the neocloud company fell more than 1% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) all climbed overnight. Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.138%, and the 30-year Treasury yield was 5.473%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.09% amid ‘bullish’ sentiment. Asian markets opened lower on Tuesday, with South Korea's KOSPI, Japan’s Nikkei 225, China’s SSE Composite and Australian stocks all trading lower at the time of writing. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of Broadcom, Inc. (AVGO) reversed overnight losses to edge up 0.3% late Monday as a 10-year cloud agreement with NTT Docomo did little to ease retail skepticism, with traders seeking a recovery catalyst after CEO Hock Tan’s AI “casino” remarks. AVGO stock rose nearly 2% on Monday to close at $334.59, snapping three straight sessions of losses. Broadcom extended its 2019 deal with Docomo, in which the companies will align their long-term tech roadmaps to advance the private cloud underpinning the Japanese telecom operator’s digital services. The company called it Broadcom Japan’s first “comprehensive” 10-year agreement covering VMware software licenses, technical assistance and maintenance support. Financial terms were not disclosed. VMware Cloud Foundation will be at the core of the infrastructure. The deal targets three priorities: keeping services available during system upgrades, strengthening security and resilience, and accelerating the delivery of new services. Docomo will use the platform to expand capacity and manage traffic spikes, improve security patching and anomaly detection, and run virtual machines and containers on a common platform. Automation across development, testing and releases will help shorten the time needed to introduce new features. The companies also plan to expand AI-driven operations and prepare the infrastructure for future developments, including 6G and IOWN. The agreement comes a week after Tan’s comments at a Singapore panel, where he called capital the biggest constraint on further AI development as Broadcom works through wafer and memory shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling,” Tan said when asked about cheaper AI models, Reuters noted. His remarks addressed investment into the broader AI sector. Tan also acknowledged that Anthropic and OpenAI had shown an ability to generate significant revenue from their latest models deployed for AI personal assistants. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk also subsequently responded, saying, “No crying in the casino,” weighing in on Tan’s concerns about speculative AI investments. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AVGO slipped to ‘extremely bearish’ at 24/100 — its lowest levels in nearly 18 months — from ‘bearish’ levels a day ago amid a 300% surge in 24-hour message volumes. Retail interest in the stock has been rising, with the ticker’s watcher base up 8% over the past three months. One user said, “The biggest problem with this stock is lack Catalysts from Broadcom, the last news was on Oct 13 for VMware HyperArmor. But nothing after it.”  Another user said, “Each time they beat earnings and revenue estimates. Yet here we are down 15% in that time frame.” A separate user said, “trash news! Still headed lower,” shortly after the Docomo agreement. Other traders were still looking for a bounce. Another user said, “when we sell off early into the session typically we see a nice reversal in overnight session into premarket.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Read Next: Tesla Stock At $4,400? Cathie Wood's ARK Pins Hopes On Robotaxis, Sees SpaceX Merger In 5 Years Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) shares fell nearly 2% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. However, Cathie Wood's ARK Investment purchased 132,498 shares of the company on Monday despite the selloff. The asset manager’s ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought 102,280 CRWV shares on Monday for $6.3 million, according to its website. The firm also bought 30,218 shares of CRWV for $1.8 million through the ARK Next Generation Technology ETF (ARKW). The purchase comes as Wall Street and Main Street remain concerned about the company’s ballooning debt levels. CoreWeave reported $35.6 billion in total debt as of June 30, while its second-quarter net interest expense rose to $640 million from $267 million a year earlier. Research and advisory firm Gartner recently said in a report that artificial intelligence infrastructure investments are in danger as concerns over bloated AI capex mount. The firm said that as the commercial duopoly for primary frontier models consolidates around Anthropic and OpenAI, the cash flows to meet that massive computing asset base from neoclouds are not scaling proportionally with upfront costs. Meanwhile, major Wall Street analysts are also taking opposing stances on CoreWeave. MoffettNathanson and BNP Paribas lowered their price targets on CoreWeave, while Goldman Sachs took a more positive outlook. MoffettNathanson slashed CRWV stock’s target to $89 from $107 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares, citing its “staggering financial obligations.” BNP Paribas also cut its price target on CoreWeave to $117 from $169 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm said that it sees a continued deterioration in investor confidence amid its debt obligations. While higher financing costs could contain the company's ability to fund future growth, the shares are "seemingly discounting some liquidity concerns," the analyst reportedly said in a research note. However, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral’ and set a price target of $106, implying upside of more than 73% from its last close. The firm said ongoing volatility in the credit market raises questions about whether CoreWeave can finance its next phase of growth, and at what pace. However, Goldman also said the ongoing debate over demand for frontier vs. off-frontier intelligence, and CoreWeave's annual recurring revenue per megawatt and unlevered internal rate of return, are "biased to the upside" over the next 24 months because of tight supply. The analyst also said that CoreWeave is differentiated from other neoclouds. Last week, Dan Ives, Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director analyst, said in an interview that the recent sell-off was an overreaction, as the broader AI demand story remains intact. “I'm not saying there's not some issues in terms as rates go higher. But given the demand, given backlog, I think this is ultimately a false narrative,” he said, while also highlighting that the sharp drop has created an opportunity for investors. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for CRWV stock was ‘extremely bullish,’ even as message volumes surged 938% over 24 hours, according to platform data. One user said, “$CRWV $NBIS are moving in tandem.. absolutely nothing to see here…” The user added, “When the wrestling match ends, these are going straight up, meanwhile, you or I have zero say in it.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. EyePoint Pharmaceuticals (EYPT), CoreWeave (CRWV) and Eos Energy Enterprises (EOSE) hit fresh 52-week lows Monday as a failed drug trial, debt refinancing concerns, and weaker full-year revenue expectations weighed on the stocks. EyePoint stock crashed 85%, while CoreWeave and Eos Energy stocks dropped 0.4% and 0.5%, respectively. EyePoint Pharmaceuticals stock crashed to a record low of $0.4 after the company reported disappointing results from LUCIA, its second pivotal Phase 3 study of DURAVYU, an experimental treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The drug failed to show that it worked as well as aflibercept in protecting vision at Weeks 52 and 56, hurting its chances of approval for the eye condition. The setback prompted the company to lay off 53% of its workforce, with the restructuring expected to bring $30 million in annualized savings and incur about $9 million in severance expenses. EyePoint reported roughly $118 million in cash and equivalents as of Sept. 30 and plans to concentrate its remaining resources on Phase 3 studies of DURAVYU for diabetic macular edema (DME). However, on Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock flipped to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bearish’. CoreWeave stock fell to a new annual low of $59.25 as analysts cut price targets amid concerns about its debt obligations and reliance on external funding. BNP Paribas lowered its price target to $117 from $169 while retaining an ‘Outperform’ rating. MoffettNathanson cut its target to $89 from $107 and maintained a ‘Neutral’ rating. The analysts highlighted the potential consequences of weaker investor confidence and expensive financing. CoreWeave needs capital to expand its data center infrastructure and support growing demand for computing capacity. Higher borrowing costs and limited access to capital markets could complicate its expansion plans and weigh on shareholder returns. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Eos Energy Enterprises stock touched a two-year low of $1.72 despite reporting preliminary third-quarter (Q3) revenue of $82 million to $83 million, a sequential growth of 19% to 21%. However, investors focused on the company’s expectation that 2026 revenue would land in the lower half of its previously announced $300 million to $350 million range. The updated outlook follows an earlier reduction in the company's revenue forecast in August. Eos has recorded eight consecutive quarters of improving gross margins, but its margins remain deeply negative as it works to increase production and improve manufacturing efficiency at its Thorn Hill facility. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘bearish’. So far this year, EYPT, CRWV and EOSE stocks have declined between 14% and 97%. Momentum investing is all about the idea of following a stock's recent trend, which can be in either direction. In the "long context," investors will essentially be "buying high, but hoping to sell even higher." And for investors following this methodology, taking advantage of trends in a stock's price is key; once a stock establishes a course, it is more than likely to continue moving in that direction. The goal is that once a stock heads down a fixed path, it will lead to timely and profitable trades. While many investors like to look for momentum in stocks, this can be very tough to define. There is a lot of debate surrounding which metrics are the best to focus on and which are poor quality indicators of future performance. The Zacks Momentum Style Score, part of the Zacks Style Scores, helps address this issue for us. title: XOM vs. BP: Which Integrated Energy Giant Has the Edge? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM and BP plc BP are two integrated energy giants with promising business prospects, supported by the prevailing strength in crude oil prices. Investors’ strong preferences for both stocks are reflected in the price chart. Over the past year, XOM has jumped 53.6%, outperforming BP’s 42.5% surge. However, the stock price performance does not necessarily establish XOM's superiority over BP as an integrated energy company. Before arriving at an investment conclusion, let's examine the broader upstream business environment, which plays a crucial role in determining the cash flow potential of both energy giants. Strong Oil Prices: A Tailwind for XOM & BP's Upstream Operations? West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is again approaching the $100-per-barrel mark, per Oilprice.com. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration, in its latest short-term energy outlook, projected WTI at $88.21 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, as is likely for BP, a British energy giant. Importantly, upstream operations generate the majority of earnings for XOM. The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Robust production from both assets has been aiding its top and bottom lines. Breakeven costs are low in both resources. Turning to BP, the British energy major’s production outlook looks bright, as its major projects, expected to begin operations between 2028 and 2030, are moving forward as planned. Once operational, these projects could help BP increase production and generate more cash. XOM vs. BP: Which Energy Giant Has a Stronger Balance Sheet? Although high oil prices are acting as a tailwind for the businesses of XOM and BP, it is also necessary to analyze the companies’ financial strength to judge how well the two energy majors could weather an unfavorable commodity pricing environment. The debt-to-capitalization of XOM is 13.73%, much lower than BP’s 43.29%. Thus, with significantly lower exposure to debt capital, ExxonMobil Holdings can sail through a tough business environment. BP, although having a relatively higher debt exposure, is also financially sound, as its debt-to-capitalization ratio is not very high. Coming to the valuation, BP stock is currently relatively cheap, as the integrated energy company is trading at a trailing 12-month EV/EBITDA multiple of 3.17x, which is lower than XOM’s 9.91x. In other words, investors are willing to pay a premium price for XOM over BP. The premium valuations reflect XOM’s strong business fundamentals, sound balance sheet and long-term growth prospects. Nevertheless, BP also presents a compelling investment case, given its relatively attractive valuation and the prevailing strength in crude oil prices, which should support its upstream profitability. title: Analysts Have Conflicting Sentiments on These Energy Companies: Antero Midstream (AM), Exxon Mobil (XOM) and Crescent Energy Company Class A (CRGY) - The Globe and Mail
content: Analysts have been eager to weigh in on the Energy sector with new ratings on Antero Midstream (AM), Exxon Mobil (XOM) and Crescent Energy Company Class A (CRGY). In a report released today, Robert Kad from Morgan Stanley maintained a Hold rating on Antero Midstream, with a price target of $26.00. The company’s shares closed last Tuesday at $20.57. According to TipRanks.com, Kad is a 4-star analyst with an average return of  7.3% and a 58.9% success rate. Kad covers the NA sector, focusing on stocks such as Enterprise Products Partners, Western Midstream Partners, and Hess Midstream Partners. Crude has staged a forceful advance, with international and domestic benchmarks pushing into triple-digit territory on a blend of supply fears and firm demand. Each leg higher has drawn attention back toward the companies that pull barrels from the ground, since their earnings move closely with the prevailing price of oil. Market participants have pointed to a tightening of available supply, trimmed output from a producer alliance, and friction along key shipping routes as forces behind the climb. As a member of the S&P 500 and one of the heaviest weights in the energy group, Exxon Mobil has become a reference point whenever the barrel makes a decisive move, and the recent direction has been firmly upward. The strength of the move has also reshaped the tone across trading desks, where the barrel's climb has become a defining feature of the sector story. For a group whose top line tracks the oil price so closely, that momentum has translated into a steady stream of attention, and each fresh move in crude has reinforced the link between the commodity and the stock. The specific development drawing the market's eye is the company's notice that it will host a conference call alongside the release of its third-quarter figures late in the month. The group also flagged, through a routine filing, that sequential movements in oil and natural-gas realizations and in refining margins would shape the quarter against the prior three-month stretch. Such snapshots are customary ahead of a major energy release, giving the market an early read on how price swings across crude, gas and refined products are likely to land. Midstream and downstream, it moves, refines and markets fuels, while a sizable chemicals arm converts hydrocarbons into plastics and other materials used across manufacturing. That breadth can steady the business through the cycle, because weakness in one link is often offset by strength in another. When crude softens, refining and chemical margins can widen as feedstock costs fall; when crude firms, the upstream arm captures the upside. This balance is a defining feature of the integrated majors and shapes how the market reads each quarterly release. The model also lets the group smooth the heavy capital demands of the business across its various arms, funding drilling in one period and refining upgrades in another. That flexibility, rooted in the scale and breadth of the operation, is part of what distinguishes the largest integrated majors from the narrower producers that populate the rest of the complex. That approach gives the ownership base a direct link to the strength of the barrel while leaving room to fund drilling, refining upgrades and chemical projects. Production volumes will show whether the upstream engine, led by the Permian, is delivering to plan, while realized prices will confirm how closely the group captured the firmer crude market. Refining and chemical margins will indicate whether the downstream arms are cushioning or amplifying the quarter. Beyond the figures, commentary on capital spending, the balance sheet and the cadence of distributions will shape how the market reads the group's direction. With crude pressing into triple digits and a flagship major about to open its books, the event sits at the intersection of a powerful commodity move and one of the energy world's most closely tracked names, ensuring the complex stays firmly in view through the reporting window. Further gains will need a fresh driver, and management named one during a July 31, 2026 call. Executives framed the asset as a turning point for Exxon’s cash. Which project is it, and what has changed there? That project is Exxon’s Guyana development, where the company has now earned back its investment. Management said during the July 31 call that the company fully recovered its $55 billion investment in the region, alongside all operating costs. Under the contract, up to 75% of production can go toward recovering that investment, and management said the remaining production is shared 50-50 with the government of Guyana. Guyana already operates at scale, pumping gross volumes of about 900,000 barrels a day during the second quarter of fiscal 2026. An analyst on the call asked whether the payback means more free cash flow or simply a smaller share of the oil. Management answered that it was “very much an inflection into free cash flow.” In the company’s view, the project has transitioned from paying back its cost to adding to Exxon’s cash. If you have held Exxon Mobil for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not the next catalyst. See how a tax-aware transition works. Guyanese operations fall under Exxon’s Upstream business. That unit generated $102 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, compared with $324 billion for the entire company. The division also houses the Permian basin, where Exxon set a second-quarter production record of more than 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels a day. A payback event like the one in Guyana ultimately surfaces in cash generation. Exxon posted free cash flow of $17.0 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, up from $5.27 billion a year earlier. That single quarter accounted for more than half of the $30.6 billion the company generated over its last four quarters. Speaking about Guyana, management said it expects twice 2025’s level of free cash flow in 2030, and the company is evaluating a ninth FPSO, a floating production ship. Exxon stock finished trading on October 20, 2026, just 0.6% below its highest close of the past year. At that level, the shares traded at 22.7 times earnings over the past four quarters, tracking closely with the 23.0 multiple for the S&P 500. That four-quarter stretch includes the second quarter, which delivered $14.5 billion of the $32.8 billion Exxon earned. The primary doubt is how much of the second quarter’s cash stemmed from oil prices rather than from Guyana. Management said that market prices ran higher than base assumptions, generating more cash sooner. Executives also stated that the conflict in the Middle East affected Exxon’s operations there, and Exxon temporarily lost about 10% of its upstream production in the quarter. The next step in Guyana has a deadline. Exxon’s fifth FPSO, Errea Wittu, set sail toward Guyana in June and remains on track to start up by the end of 2026, management said. That leaves two things to watch: Exxon’s free cash flow in its third-quarter report, expected on or around October 30, 2026, and the start-up of Errea Wittu before the end of 2026.  moved into sharper focus as crude climbed sharply on supply concerns during a busy earnings week, lifting a broad base of energy names before a later easing spurred rotation across the tape. As megacap technology names swung hard through a crowded run of quarterly updates, money leaned toward the oil majors, and the largest integrated producer on the American market drew a fresh bid alongside firmer barrels. Trading desks framed the stretch as a search for ballast while the technology complex churned. Crude sits at the heart of the energy complex, so a sharp climb in the barrel tends to ripple quickly through the producers that pull it from the ground. When oil firms, the output each field delivers fetches a stronger price, lifting the cash a large producer can generate without any change to the barrels it lifts. That leverage to the barrel is a defining feature of the energy arena. A steady climb in crude can lift the reported earnings of an upstream producer faster than the move in oil itself, because the cost of lifting each barrel stays broadly fixed while the sale price rises. The upstream arm finds and produces crude oil and natural gas across a spread of regions, feeding the barrels that anchor the group's earnings. The downstream arm refines that crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, while the chemical arm converts feedstocks into plastics and specialty materials sold into countless end markets. This integrated design is the hallmark of the business. When crude is strong, the upstream arm drives earnings; when margins on refined fuels widen, the downstream arm carries more weight; and the chemical arm adds a thread tied to broad industrial demand. An integrated energy group captures value at several stages of the chain at after, and that breadth tends to smooth the swings that buffet a pure upstream producer. When crude slides, cheaper feedstock can lift refining and chemical margins, so the downstream arms can cushion a softer barrel, lending the whole group a steadier character across the cycle. That balance cuts the other way too. When crude climbs sharply, as it did this week, the upstream arm shines while refining faces costlier input, yet the combined base still leans toward the firmer barrel. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. The deepwater development has moved from early finds to steady production, adding a large and growing stream of barrels to the group's base. The Guyana play matters because its barrels come at a competitive cost and from a region where the group holds a commanding position alongside its partners. That offshore engine gives the name a clear growth thread distinct from the mature fields that make up much of the sector. As crude firmed this week, the scale and low cost of the Guyana barrels drew particular attention, since they feed directly into how the market reads the group's expanding production footprint. Alongside its offshore reach, the group holds a deep position in the Permian basin, the vast shale region straddling the American Southwest that has become the engine of domestic oil growth. A large acreage base there feeds a steady stream of barrels that the group can dial up or down with relative speed compared with long-cycle offshore projects. Shale output answers to drilling that can be ramped quickly, giving the group a flexible lever to lean into firmer crude. The Permian barrels sit close to the group's refining and chemical plants along the coast, a proximity that trims transport and knits the upstream and downstream arms more tightly together. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM) has a set of advantages that most smaller oil companies can only dream of. Its business stretches across exploration, production, refining, chemicals, and specialty products. This means ExxonMobil can make money at every step of the energy chain, instead of relying only on the ups and downs of crude oil prices. What really sets ExxonMobil apart are three things: its massive scale, the way it ties all its operations together, and the valuable assets it owns. Big projects in Guyana's deepwater fields and the Permian Basin let ExxonMobil boost production at a good price. Its vast refining network, in-house technology, and worldwide logistics make the company extra efficient, something newcomers can't easily copy. Plus, its strong balance sheet and easy access to capital mean it can take on big projects that might take years before they pay off. That combination of scale and income potential also makes it worth comparing with other established dividend payers featured in Top 10 Unstoppable Dividend Stocks to Buy. Still, even with all these advantages, ExxonMobil isn't immune to trouble. When oil prices drop, the whole business feels it. There's always the risk that huge investments or new environmental rules could eat into profits. Also read: 10 Best Battery Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM) is trading at a forward P/E of 14.77, compared to a trailing P/E of 20.75. That difference shows analysts think earnings are set to climb, which equates to a forward earnings yield of about 6.8%. That's a fair valuation for a company as large as ExxonMobil, but it's not exactly cheap. Just a few months ago, its forward P/E was 12.08. For comparison, Chevron is currently trading at a forward multiple of around 15.20. The big question is whether ExxonMobil's growth and improved efficiency can really justify this higher price. And with the 10-year Treasury yield recently moving above 5%, the extra return you get from ExxonMobil isn't that much higher, so investors are not being paid a big premium for taking on the risks of the oil business. ExxonMobil's next earnings report comes out on October 30, 2026. Until then, it's worth watching market expectations closely, especially since recent boosts in refining profits were helped by geopolitical issues that might not stick around. Also take a look at: BP (BP) vs Exxon Mobil (XOM): Which Oil Major is a Better Buy? ExxonMobil's dividend is known more for its reliability than for a big payout. The company pays an annual dividend of $4.12 per share, which works out to a 2.30% yield and a payout ratio of 52.51%. That yield is a lot lower than its five-year average of 3.38%, meaning the stock price has grown faster than the dividend itself. Even then, the stock stands out among other dividend stocks gaining this year, because of its Dividend Aristocrat status. The payout ratio gives ExxonMobil a decent buffer if earnings dip, but it's not the whole picture for a big oil company. Dividends only work if there's enough cash left after running the business, paying taxes, and investing in new projects. In the first half of 2026, ExxonMobil paid out $8.6 billion in dividends. Its most recent report also showed a conservative net-debt-to-capital ratio of 10.7% as of June, which means the company has the flexibility to keep paying dividends even if times get tough. ExxonMobil also has an impressive history of raising its dividend. As of January 2026, it's boosted its annual dividend per share for 43 straight years, including a 4% bump in the fourth quarter of 2025. That kind of track record matters, since growing dividends help investors keep up with inflation and boost their returns on what they originally paid. Of course, just because the company's raised its dividend in the past doesn't mean it always will, especially if oil prices fall or big spending needs pop up. But there's more to owning ExxonMobil than just the dividend. The total return, meaning the combination of dividends, share buybacks, and price appreciation, matters a lot. In 2025, ExxonMobil returned $37.2 billion to shareholders, split between $17.2 billion in dividends and $20 billion in buybacks. Buybacks can help boost earnings per share, but they're not guaranteed. How much the company buys back depends on cash flow and what's happening in the market. With a 2.30% yield, ExxonMobil isn't paying out as much as it has in the past. The dividend looks safe for now, but the stock price doesn't leave much of a cushion if oil prices take a hit. The stock is a better fit for investors looking for steady, long-term growth and rising income, rather than those chasing a high yield right away. ExxonMobil's strengths, including its competitive edge, valuable assets, and integrated approach, help support a reliable dividend. But with the stock price climbing lately, there's less of a safety net for new investors. The shares make the most sense for people who want steady, long-term exposure to the energy sector and a dividend that can grow over time, not just for those looking for a quick boost in income. After climbing steeply on worries that global supply could tighten, benchmark prices drifted lower as those fears cooled and the market weighed fresh barrels coming onto the scene. For an integrated group, a softer crude price cuts both ways. While crude slipped, refining margins stayed firm, a detail that mattered for the downstream business. Refining spreads measure the difference between the cost of crude fed into a plant and the value of the gasoline, diesel and jet fuel that come out. When those spreads stay healthy even as crude eases, the refining arm can lean into the gap. Firm margins across the refining slate help steady group-wide earnings during stretches when crude prices wobble, and that cushioning effect is a core reason the integrated model has stayed in favor through many cycles in the oil and gas sector. An integrated energy group knits together activities that are often split across separate companies. Refining and marketing sit at the other, turning raw barrels into the fuels that move cars, trucks, ships and planes. In the middle lies a chemicals arm that converts hydrocarbons into the building blocks of plastics, packaging and countless everyday goods. The design is meant to smooth the ride. When crude is strong, the production side shines; when crude softens, refining and chemicals often take up the slack. The upstream arm remains the engine that initial reacts to any shift in crude. Here the group manages a broad base of oil and gas fields, blending mature assets that throw off steady cash with newer developments designed to add fresh barrels. The mix spans onshore shale, deepwater projects and large conventional fields, giving the production book a spread across geographies and reservoir types. A softer crude price tends to sharpen attention on the cost of each barrel. Operators that can keep a lid on drilling and completion costs are better placed to keep cash flowing when prices cool. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. Among the group's production assets, the Permian basin in the United States occupies a central place. Expanded positions there have lifted the share of barrels that come from short-cycle shale, which can be dialed up or trimmed as prices move. Beyond the Permian, the company carries a global base of barrels, from offshore developments to large gas ventures feeding liquefied natural gas trade. Refining turns barrels into fuels, capturing the spread between crude costs and fuel values. Chemicals take hydrocarbons a step further, producing the resins and compounds that feed packaging, construction and consumer goods. Both businesses tend to breathe on different rhythms than the upstream arm. With refining margins firm as crude eased, the downstream side offered a steadying presence. Chemicals, meanwhile, track their own cycle tied to industrial activity and the cost of feedstock. Oil and gas names tend to trade in loose lockstep with the benchmark, rising when supply fears flare and easing when those fears fade. Against that backdrop, the largest integrated names often act as anchors. Their scale, diversified earnings and steady dividends give the market a reference point when crude churns. Softer crude trims the value of fresh barrels, while firm refining margins reward the plants that turn those barrels into fuel. Large integrated names embody both sides, which is why they often steady the tone of energy trading when the benchmark lurches. The recent run-up in crude traced back to worries that global supply might tighten faster than fresh barrels could fill the gap. Disruptions, geopolitics and shifting production plans among major exporters can all feed that kind of anxiety, and prices tend to spike when the market frets about scarcity. The subsequent easing reflected a calmer read on those same concerns. For a group that both produces and refines, the swing is a study in balance. A sharp climb rewards the production arm but squeezes refining as feedstock costs jump.
